The Philadelphia 76ers are based in the Philadelphia metropolitan area.
The 76ers compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA).
The 76ers play their home games at the Wells Fargo Center located in South Philadelphia Sports Complex.
Founded in 1946, the 76ers are one of the oldest franchises in the NBA and one of only 8 out of 23 to survive the league's first decade.
Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment (HBSE) owns and manages the 76ers, with founders Josh Harris and David Blitzer acquiring the team in 2011.

The 76ers have had a prominent history, including many Hall of Fame players such as Dolph Schayes, Hal Greer, Wilt Chamberlain, Chet Walker, Billy Cunningham, George McGinnis, Julius Erving, Maurice Cheeks, Bobby Jones, Moses Malone, Charles Barkley, and Allen Iverson.

The 76ers have won three NBA championships. Their first came in 1955 under their previous name, the Syracuse Nationals. The second title was in 1967 with Wilt Chamberlain leading the team. The third title was in 1983 with Julius Erving and Moses Malone.
The 76ers have only been back to the NBA Finals once since 2001, when they lost to the Los Angeles Lakers in five games led by Allen Iverson.
Chamberlain, Erving, Malone, Iverson, and Joel Embiid have been named the NBA's Most Valuable Player while playing for the 76ers, for a total of seven MVP awards.
1946–1963: Syracuse Nationals
Billy Gabor joined the Syracuse Nationals in 1948.
Dolph Schayes joined the team in 1949 and spent his entire career with the team, winning a championship together in 1955.
1958–59: Syracuse Nationals
Hal Greer joined the Nationals in 1958 and spent his entire 15-season career with the franchise; he won a championship with the team in 1967.
Danny Biasone established the Syracuse Nationals of the National Basketball League (NBL) in Syracuse, New York, for $5,000 in 1946.
The Nationals put together a 21–23 record and finished fourth in the playoffs against the Rochester Royals in four games during their first season in the NBL.
In the second season of 1947–48, the Nationals struggled with a 24–36 record but made it to the playoffs where they were swept by Anderson Duffey Packers in three straight games.
1948–1950: Syracuse Nationals
Leo Ferris was recruited for the team prior to the 1948–49 season.

Al Cervi signed on as player-coach and outbid the New York Knicks for Dolph Schayes, who made his professional debut with the Nationals in 1949. The Nationals won a winning record for the first time with a 40–23 record.
In the playoffs, the Nationals defeated Hammond Calumet Buccaneers in two straight games but lost to Anderson Duffey Packers in four games during their second season.
1950–1951: Syracuse Nationals
The Nationals played mediocre basketball all season and finished fourth with a 32–34 record.

In the playoffs, the Nationals stunned the first-place Philadelphia Warriors by winning two straight games. In the Eastern Finals, they were beaten by the New York Knickerbockers in a five-game series.
1951–1952: Syracuse Nationals
Leo Ferris emphasized a patient offense and scrappy defense which led the league with 79.5 points per game as the Nationals won the Eastern Division.
In the playoffs, the Nationals knocked off the Philadelphia Warriors again in three games to reach the NBA Finals.
1952–1953: Syracuse Nationals
The Nationals finished second place in a hard-fought 3-way battle for first place with a record of 47–24.
In the playoffs, they faced Boston Celtics and lost Game 1 at home 87–81. Needing a win to keep their hopes alive, they took the Celtics deep into overtime before losing in quadruple OT 111–105.
1953–1954: Syracuse Nationals
The Nationals acquired Alex Groza and Ralph Beard as Indianapolis Olympians folded.

Once again, the Nationals battled for the Division title falling two games short with a 42–30 record. In the playoffs, they won all four games of a round-robin tournament involving three playoff teams from the East.
1954–1955: Syracuse Nationals
The NBA struggled financially and down to just 8 teams during this season.

Biasone suggested limiting shot time to speed up the game and increase scoring. The 24-second shot clock was implemented, leading to an instant success as scoring increased by 14 points per game league-wide.
1955–1956: Syracuse Nationals
Coming off their NBA Championship, the Nationals struggled during this season needing a tiebreaker over Knickerbockers to avoid finishing last and make playoffs with a 35–37 record.
In the playoffs, they stunned the Celtics winning the first-round series in three games by taking final two games.
1956–1957: Syracuse Nationals
Paul Seymour replaced Cervi as coach. Under Seymour, the Nationals rebounded to finish second place with a 38–34 record.
In the playoffs, they had trouble knocking off the defending champion Warriors and advanced to Eastern Finals with two straight wins but were swept by eventual champions Celtics.
1957–1958: Syracuse Nationals
Fort Wayne and Rochester moved on to Detroit and Cincinnati for this season leaving the Syracuse Nationals as last small-town team in big city NBA.
The Nationals held their own finishing second place with a 41–31 record. In playoffs, they lost first round against Philadelphia Warriors.
1958–1959: Syracuse Nationals
Despite a mediocre 35–37 record for this season the Nationals made playoffs by finishing third place.
In the playoffs, they swept Knickerbockers in two straight to reach Eastern Finals where they lost to eventual champion Celtics alternating wins before losing Game 7.
1960–1961: Syracuse Nationals
The Lakers relocated from Minneapolis to Los Angeles for this season making the Syracuse Nationals last old NBL team still playing in original city.
The Nationals went on to make playoffs again by finishing third place with a 38–41 record. They were dangerous in playoffs as they stunned Warriors in three straight games.
1961–1962: Syracuse Nationals
Hal Greer led the way with 22.8 points per game while Schayes missed 24 games during this season.
The Nationals finished third place again with a 41–39 record. In playoffs, they lost first two games to Warriors on road and won next two forcing fifth game in Philadelphia.
1962–1963: Syracuse Nationals
Johnny Kerr's scrappy play helped the Nationals finish second place for this season with a 48–32 record.
In playoffs, they faced Cincinnati Royals getting off to 2-1 series lead. Needing one win to advance to Eastern Finals again, they lost two straight dropping decisive fifth game in overtime.
The playoff loss on March 26, 1963, proved to be the last game for Syracuse Nationals as investors Irv Kosloff and Ike Richman purchased team from Danny Biasone.
They moved the team to Philadelphia filling void left by Warriors who had moved to San Francisco. The NBA thus returned to Philadelphia one year after Warriors' departure.

1964–65: Wilt Chamberlain era
The 76ers acquired legendary Wilt Chamberlain from Warriors in this season; he led the team to NBA title in 1967.
In semifinals, they pushed Celtics to seven games with 110-109 lead in Game 7. After Hal Greer's pass was stolen by John Havlicek, Celtics beat Los Angeles Lakers and won NBA Championship.
1965–66: Wilt Chamberlain era
The 76ers had a dream season starting 46-4 with record of 68-13.
Chamberlain, Billy Cunningham, Greer, all-stars Chet Walker, Lucious Jackson and Wali Jones led the team to semifinals.
1966–67: First title in Philadelphia
Led by head coach Alex Hannum, the 76ers had a dream season starting 46-4 with record of 68-13.
Chamberlain, Billy Cunningham, Greer, all-stars Chet Walker, Lucious Jackson and Wali Jones led the team to semifinals where they beat Celtics in five games.
1967–68: First year at the Spectrum
With a new home court in form of The Spectrum to defend their championship, 76ers made it back to playoffs.
In rematch of previous year's semifinals, 76ers held 3-1 series lead over Celtics before Celtics staged dramatic comeback beating 76ers in seven games.
Billy Cunningham played nine seasons with 76ers from 1965 to 1972 and later coached team for eight seasons from 1977 to 1985.
The Chamberlain trade was followed by a freefall in performance, which Ramsay accelerated by divestiture of All-Star forward Chet Walker to Chicago Bulls.
1970–71: Fall of the 76ers
The 76ers struggled with a 32-76 record under head coach Paul Seymour.
In playoffs, they lost first two games to Warriors on road and won next two forcing fifth game in Philadelphia. In Game 5, Warriors ended season with 121-104 victory.
Julius Erving played 11 seasons with the 76ers from 1976 to 1987.
The 76ers finally came all the way back in 1976-77, largely due to ABA-NBA merger. The Nets' franchise player Julius Erving was traded for $3 million by the 76ers.
1976–77: Julius Erving era
Led by Erving, the 76ers began an exciting ride beating Boston Celtics in seven-game playoff series.
They defeated Houston Rockets led by future 76er Moses Malone in six games to advance to NBA Finals. In Finals, they lost first two games but won next four to give title to Portland Trail Blazers.
1978–79: Julius Erving era
The 76ers returned to playoffs after five-year absence.
They were defeated by defending champion Pistons in three games.
Moses Malone won MVP honors in 1983, leading the 76ers to their first title in 16 years. Harold Katz bought the 76ers from Dixon in 1981.
On watch, the final piece of championship puzzle was completed before 1982-83 season when they acquired center Moses Malone from Houston Rockets.
1982–83: Third NBA championship
Led by Hall of Famers Julius Erving, Maurice Cheeks and All-Stars Andrew Toney and Bobby Jones, the 76ers dominated regular season winning 65 games.
Moses Malone was named League MVP. When asked how playoffs would run, he answered "four, four, four" meaning they needed to win four in each of three rounds.
After disappointing 1983-84 season which ended with five-game loss to upstart New Jersey Nets, Charles Barkley arrived for the 1984-85 season.
For next eight seasons, he brought delight to Philadelphia fans thanks to his humorous and sometimes controversial ways.
1986–87: Post-MVP era
On June 16, 1986, Katz made two of most controversial personnel moves in franchise history by trading Moses Malone to Washington and first overall pick from San Diego Clippers to Cleveland Cavaliers.
Roy Hinson, Jeff Ruland, Cliff Robinson were received. Cleveland turned acquired pick into future All-Star Brad Daugherty.
1987–88: Post-MVP era
With team's record at 20-23, Jim Lynam replaced assistant coach Guokas.
Lynam finished season 16-23 to bring Philadelphia overall mark to 36-46. For first time since 1974-75, the 76ers failed to reach playoffs.
1988–89: Post-MVP era
Philadelphia returned to playoffs after one-year absence but was swept by New York Knicks in first round.
In 1989-90, Barkley finished second in league MVP voting as 76ers won Atlantic Division title with 53-29 record.
Ed Snider purchased the 76ers in 1996. Lynam relinquished head coaching position to become general manager following 1991-92 season.
He hired Doug Moe who lasted just 56 games with 19-37 record. Popular former player and longtime assistant coach Fred Carter succeeded Moe as head coach in March 1993.
1996–1997: Post-MVP era
Lynam relinquished his head coaching position to become general manager following the 1991-92 season.
He hired Doug Moe who lasted just 56 games with a 19-37 record. Popular former player and longtime assistant coach Fred Carter succeeded Moe as head coach in March 1993.
1996–1998: Post-MVP era
The 76ers won lottery for top pick in 1996 NBA draft.
Questions remained, but with first pick, the 76ers selected Allen Iverson who was nicknamed "the Answer".
01 season: NBA Finals loss to Lakers
Allen Iverson won MVP honors while leading 76ers to NBA Finals. Larry Brown coached from 1997 to 2003 and was named Coach of the Year in 2001.
During 2000-01 season, the 76ers got off hot start by winning first ten games.
07: Post-MVP era
Allen Iverson gave ultimatum to management in December 2006.
On December 19, 2006, Allen Iverson and Ivan McFarlin were sent to Denver Nuggets for Andre Miller, Joe Smith, two first-round picks.
Brett Brown coached the team from 2013 to 2020.
Jerry Colangelo joined front office in 2015. Joel Embiid and Ben Simmons were considered centerpieces of future.
15 season: Post-MVP era
Tony Wroten, guard for the 76ers, referred to major rebuilding culture as "The Process".
During 2013 draft, the 76ers agreed in principle to trade All-Star Jrue Holiday and 42nd pick to New Orleans Pelicans for Nerlens Noel and Pelicans' 2014 first-round pick.
16 season: Post-MVP era
Sam Hinkie, who had previously worked for Houston Rockets, was named general manager.
The Sixers drastically changed logo and colors in effort to appeal to hip-hop-oriented culture. Red, white and blue were retained as trim.
18 season: Post-MVP era
The 76ers finished regular season third place with a 52-30 winning record.
In first round, they defeated Heat in five games to win their first playoff series since 2011.
19 season: Post-MVP era
Jimmy Butler was traded from the 76ers for Josh Richardson and Horford. The team also signed Al Horford.
21 season: Post-MVP era
The Sixers finished regular season as third seed with a 51-31 record.
In playoffs, they were eliminated by Celtics in four games. Head coach Brett Brown was fired on August 24.
22 season: Post-MVP era
James Harden and Paul Millsap were acquired from Brooklyn Nets for Simmons, Andre Drummond, Seth Curry, two first-round picks.
The Sixers finished the season as third seed with a record of 54-28. They defeated Wizards in five games but lost to Atlanta Hawks in seven.
That offseason, Paul George signed four-year max contract deal with the Sixers.
They also resigned Kyle Lowry and acquired Eric Gordon.
The Philadelphia 76ers' original logo featured a stylized red "7" and blue "6" with 13 stars above the "7".
The home white uniform now had a thick red band across abdomen, while road uniform featured red tops and blue shorts.
The Sixers returned to wearing blue uniforms on the road. After sporting "PHILA" on chest for eight seasons, the uniform now read "Sixers" in Art Deco style lettering.
Starting with 1978-79 season, the Sixers wore cleaner uniform design reminiscent of late 60s outfits. Side stripes were eliminated and team logo was emblazoned on right leg.
